facts.statement: Jaklapallisaurus is a type of unaysaurid sauropodomorph dinosaur.
facts.quote: Jaklapallisaurus is a genus of unaysaurid sauropodomorph dinosaur.

facts.statement: Jaklapallisaurus lived in what is now central India during the Late Triassic period, specifically from the late Norian to the earliest Rhaetian.
facts.quote: It lived during the Late Triassic period (late Norian to earliest Rhaetian) in what is now Telangana, central India.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Jaklapallisaurus was collected from the Upper Maleri Formation in the Pranhita–Godavari Basin.
facts.quote: The Jaklapallisaurus holotype specimen, ISI R274, consists of postcranial material which was collected from the Upper Maleri Formation (late Norian–earliest Rhaetian) of the Pranhita–Godavari Basin.

facts.statement: Jaklapallisaurus was first named by Fernando E. Novas, Martin D. Ezcurra, Sankar Chatterjee, and Tharavat S. Kutty in 2011.
facts.quote: It was first named by Fernando E. Novas, Martin D. Ezcurra, Sankar Chatterjee and Tharavat S. Kutty in 2011.

facts.statement: The species name 'asymmetricus' refers to the highly asymmetrical astragalus bone seen from the distal end.
facts.quote: The specific name refers to the highly asymmetrical astragalus of this species in distal view.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analysis places Jaklapallisaurus as the sister taxon to Macrocollum within the family Unaysauridae.
facts.quote: Ezcurra et al. performed a phylogenetic analysis of bagualosaurians, recovering it as the sister taxon to Macrocollum, in a clade also containing Unaysaurus, called Unaysauridae.

facts.statement: Jaklapallisaurus lived between 227.3 and 201.4 million years ago during the Norian to Rhaetian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Norian to Rhaetian (227.3 to 201.4 million years ago)

rejected.statement: In 2023, the specific epithet was corrected from 'asymmetrica' to 'asymmetricus' to match the masculine gender of the genus name.
rejected.quote: In 2023, the ending of the Latinized specific epithet was changed from the female 'asymmetrica' to the masculine 'asymmetricus' because the ending of the Latinized genus Jakalapallisaurus is masculine.
